content: Copper deficiency can lead to a clinical syndrome characterized by anemia or pancytopenia and neurodegeneration in humans and other mammals. In affected animals, symptoms such as ataxia and spasticity are observed. Although cases of human anemia caused by copper deficiency are rare, they have been documented for many years. More recently, a syndrome resembling swayback disease in ruminants has been identified in humans. Individuals with this condition develop progressive spasticity, ataxia, and neuropathy, which may also be accompanied by anemia. The clinical presentation of copper deficiency in humans closely mimics subacute combined degeneration, a well-recognized and relatively common condition caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. In ruminants, copper deficiency is often due to grazing on copper-deficient lands or consuming copper-poor feed. In humans, copper deficiency can result from inadequate copper in parenteral nutrition or as a consequence of gastric bypass surgery. The typical American diet, which provides approximately 9 mg of copper daily, may still be insufficient in some cases. Additionally, zinc competes with copper for absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Chronic excessive zinc intake, such as that seen in individuals who overuse denture adhesive products containing zinc, can lead to copper deficiency.
